lesson_title: Taps and Drains: the Four-Sector Circular Flow
hook_text: The whole South African economy fits in one bath with the plug half out.
clip_script: Picture a bath. Plug half out. Taps running. The LEVEL of the water is the size of the economy — national income. Three drains pull money out. You save some of your wage: it sits in the bank instead of at the till. You pay tax: the payslip is smaller than the wage. You buy something imported: that money boards a plane. Save, tax, import. Three taps pour money in. A business borrows and builds a warehouse — that's investment. Government spends on a clinic, a road, teachers. And the world buys our coal and our cars — exports. Now the only rule: the bath sits still when the taps TOGETHER match the drains TOGETHER. Not tap for drain. Together. So what's a recession? A tap closes. The world stops buying — goods sit unsold, a shift gets cut, wages shrink, less gets spent at the spaza, so the spaza orders less. And here's the part people miss: the bath DOES settle again — but lower. Poorer people save less, pay less tax, buy fewer imports, so the drains narrow until everything balances. Balanced, and a lot of people out of work. Balance is not the same as good.
visual_style: A single deep bath rendered as a township street scene: taps labelled as a warehouse, a clinic and a container ship; drains labelled as a bank, a payslip and an aeroplane; the waterline dropping and settling as a shift is cut.
mood: Calm and clear, tightening into hard truth.
pacing: Unhurried through the three drains and three taps, then quickening round by round as the level falls, ending on a still line.
